fermentables.name: Dextrose (Corn Sugar)
fermentables.description: Glucose monohydrate — the water of crystallisation is why it is 42 PPG rather than 46. The standard priming sugar.
fermentables.usageNotes: Yeast take it first and fastest; completely neutral in flavour.
fermentables.attribution: No source. USDA's SR Legacy set has no dextrose entry, and the ppg of 42 stored here was never cited to anything. It is the figure every brewing text gives for dextrose monohydrate, and it follows from the hydrate: C6H12O6.H2O is 90.9% anhydrous glucose by mass, so 46 x 0.909 = 41.8. That arithmetic is sound but it is this project's arithmetic, not a published measurement, so the number comes out until there is a document behind it.

fermentables.name: Belgian Candi Sugar (Clear)
fermentables.description: Crystallised sucrose used to boost gravity in Belgian tripels and golden strongs without adding body.
fermentables.sourceNote: Sugar is sugar, and that is the whole point of this record: at 46 ppg it is the reference the entire scale is defined against, so there is nothing for a maker to add. What is not sourced is the colour. 1 degree Lovibond is a reasonable description of a colourless crystal but no document here establishes it, and the EU directive expresses sugar colour in ICUMSA units rather than Lovibond, so it cannot be converted across. Note also that "clear candi sugar" is sold both as rock-candy crystals and as a pale syrup; this record is the crystallised form. A syrup of the same name carries water and cannot be 46.
fermentables.attribution: Clear Belgian candi sugar is crystallised beet sucrose - the pale grades are sugar, not a caramel - so its extract is the extract of sugar and does not need a vendor to assert it. USDA FoodData Central, Sugars, granulated (SR Legacy, FDC ID 169655): 99.98 g of carbohydrate and 99.8 g of total sugars per 100 g, against 0.02 g of water. The sugars figure is Analytical from 7 samples and the water figure Analytical from 8. This project's method is 46 x available carbohydrate, so 46 x 0.9998 is 46.0 ppg, which confirms the stored 46 exactly. The identity is also fixed in law: Annex A point 2 of EU Directive 2001/111/EC defines sugar as "purified and crystallised sucrose of sound and fair marketable quality". The record previously cited the Candi Syrup Inc homepage, which answers automated requests with 429 and in any case says nothing about composition.

fermentables.name: Belgian Candi Syrup D-180
fermentables.description: Deeply caramelised Belgian syrup contributing dark fruit and burnt-sugar complexity to dubbels and quads.
fermentables.sourceNote: Extract barely moves across the grades and colour moves a lot, which is the useful thing to know: D-45, D-90 and D-180 are the same sugar at about the same dry matter, browned further each time. Pick the grade for colour and flavour, not for gravity. Note also that browning consumes sugar - the melanoidins and other reaction products are dry matter but not fermentable extract - so all three of these ppg figures are ceilings rather than promises, and the darker the grade the wider that gap is likely to be.
fermentables.attribution: No citation for the extract figure, and the reason is worth setting out because the product is simpler than its absence suggests. Dark candi syrup is beet sucrose taken through a browning reaction, so its dry solids are sugar and sugar-derived; the only thing standing between that and a ppg is how much water the syrup carries. The stored 32 implies about 70% dry matter. Law bounds it but does not fix it: Annex A of EU Directive 2001/111/EC requires a sugar solution or invert sugar syrup to be "not less than 62% by weight" dry matter, which is 28.5 ppg, and the stored 32 sits above that floor. The directive cannot do more than bound it, because a syrup at 180 Lovibond is far darker than the "not more than 45 ICUMSA units" its point 4 allows - a caramelised syrup falls outside the definitions entirely. Candi Syrup Inc answers automated requests with 429 across retries, so their own figure could not be read.

fermentables.name: Lactose (Milk Sugar)
fermentables.description: Brewing yeast cannot ferment lactose at all — it stays in the beer as residual sweetness and body. The defining ingredient of milk stouts and modern pastry/milkshake styles.
fermentables.usageNotes: 0% fermentable: it raises OG and FG equally and does not add alcohol. Not vegan; and note that Saccharomyces cannot touch it but Kluyveromyces marxianus can.
fermentables.sourceNote: The ppg on this record is unsourced and the citation is a homepage. Briess was cited but their site publishes a single page in its sitemap and no product specification for lactose. USDA FoodData Central has no entry for pure lactose either - searching it returns lactose-free milks and infant formulas, not the sugar - so the nutrition-panel method this project uses for adjuncts has nothing to work from. Worth noting that the stored 35 looks low on its face: lactose monohydrate is about 95% anhydrous sugar by weight, which on the 46-point sucrose scale would be nearer 44. That is arithmetic, not a source, and the figure has been left alone rather than changed on the strength of it.
fermentables.attribution: No citation, because the company cited does not make this. briess.com was the source on this record; Briess's actual brewing catalogue is at brewingwithbriess.com, and its product sitemap lists 90 products with no lactose among them - they make malt extracts, specialty malts and a sorghum extract. USDA FoodData Central has no entry for pure lactose either; searching it returns lactose-free milks and infant formulas. So the nutrition-panel method this project uses for adjuncts has nothing to work from and the dose figures here are unsourced. Worth recording that the stored 35 ppg looks low on its face: lactose monohydrate is about 95% anhydrous sugar by weight, which on the 46-point sucrose scale would be nearer 44. That is arithmetic, not a source, so the figure has been left alone.

fermentables.name: Maltodextrin
fermentables.description: Unfermentable glucose polymer added purely for body and mouthfeel; flavourless and non-sweet.
fermentables.attribution: ppg is derived from the Nutrition Facts panel of a pure maltodextrin powder as filed with USDA FoodData Central (Branded Foods, FDC ID 2585907, "UNFLAVORED MALTODEXTRIN POWDER", PepsiCo Inc. / CytoSport, published 29 June 2023, single ingredient: maltodextrin): a 56 g serving declaring 53 g of total carbohydrate and no fibre. This project's method is 46 x (total carbohydrate - fibre) / serving grams, so 46 x 53 / 56 = 43.5, against a stored 40. A second, independent panel agrees: FDC ID 2423905, also single-ingredient maltodextrin, declares 14 g of carbohydrate in a 15 g serving, which is 42.9. The two bracket the figure at 43, and the difference between them is label rounding on the smaller serving. The citation is the data endpoint rather than the portal page, which FDC serves from a client-side router and returns 404 to anything that is not a browser.
fermentables.sourceNote: The panel backs ppg and nothing else. Maltodextrin is close to pure carbohydrate, so its gravity contribution is near sucrose's 46 - the stored 40 understated it by about 8%. What the panel cannot tell you is the part that actually matters for brewing: dextrose equivalent. Maltodextrins are sold from about DE 4 to DE 20, and the higher the DE the more of that carbohydrate brewing yeast can ferment, but DE is not a food-labelling quantity and neither panel states it. The fermentability figure on this record is therefore unsourced, and so is the colour. Both panels are for food-grade powder rather than a brewing-branded product; the molecule is the same, the DE may not be.

fermentables.name: Invert Sugar No. 3
fermentables.description: Graded British invert syrup (No.1 pale through No.4 dark); No.3 brings rich caramel and dried fruit to old ales and porters.
fermentables.attribution: Ragus Sugars, Invert Sugar Syrup, product page: a full invert is manufactured to 76 Brix with a polarisation of -18 to -22, and a partial invert to a maximum of 77 Brix at +17 to +23. Brix here is dissolved solids, which for an invert syrup is sugar, so 46 x 0.76 is 35.0 ppg against a stored 36.
fermentables.sourceNote: The citation was pointed at the wrong company and the replacement only covers half the record. Crisp Malt was cited for this, but Crisp publish no invert sugar at all - it is absent from their malts sitemap and their own site search for "invert" returns no product. Ragus is a British sugar refiner that does make brewing inverts and does publish a specification, so the dissolved-solids figure and the ppg derived from it now rest on that. What Ragus do not publish is the numbered grade system: No. 1 through No. 4 are colour grades, darkening with each boil, and the stored 55 Lovibond for a No. 3 is not supported by this or any document this project holds. Treat the colour as unsourced.
